thanks.
Jack

Hi Jack,

You are using lattice, so I am not sure why you are posting to the
ggplot2 list (unless you wanted us to give you a ggplot2 solution?).
Anyway, I think the below might do what you want. You should be able
to cut and paste into your console and run it.

Hope this helps,

Josh

################### Code ####################

## Read in your data
test <- read.table(textConnection("

C,C7,1,96.8,6,0.91"), sep = ",", header = TRUE,
stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
closeAllConnections()

## Convert 'Product' to a factor with levels ordered by
## Catergory (alphabetically), then weight (numerically)
## (btw, it is spelled "Category" not "Catergory")
test$Product <- with(test, factor(Product,
levels = Product[order(Catergory, weight)]))

## Create a new variable with purple, blue, or green
## depending on whether Catergory matches A, B, or C
test$CatCol <-
c("purple", "blue", "green")[match(test$Catergory, c("A", "B", "C"))]

## look at the structure of the final data
## I find it convenient to be consistent in my variable naming
## scheme such as whether it is upper or lower case as this makes
## it easier for me to remember what to type without checking
str(test)

## Convert data to long format so that conditioning can be used
ltest <- reshape(data = test, direction = "long", varying =
list(c("weightcount", "ratingcount"),
c("weight", "Rating")),
v.names = c("Count", "Value"),
times = c("weight", "rating"), timevar = "variable")

## look at the structure of the long data
str(ltest)

require(lattice)

## create a both plots conditioning on the variable
## note the addition of the scales argument to let the x axis
## freely vary, and the slightly more complex specification of the origin
both.plots <- barchart(Product ~ Value | variable, data = ltest,
stack = FALSE, rectangles = TRUE, horizontal = TRUE,
ylab = "Product", xlab = "Value", col = ltest$CatCol,
main = "Weight and Rating of all samples", border = "NA",
scales = list(x = list(relation = "free")),
panel = function(x, y, subscripts, ...) {
panel.grid(h = 0, v = -1, col = "gray")
panel.barchart(x, y, origin = ifelse(
ltest$variable[subscripts][1] == "weight", 100, 0), ...)
panel.text((x * 1.01), y,
label = paste(ltest$Count[subscripts]),
cex = 0.7)
})

## create a simple plot of just the weights
weight.plot <- barchart(Product ~ weight, data = test,
layout = c(1, 1), stack = FALSE, rectangles = TRUE, horizontal = TRUE,
ylab = "Product", xlab = "weight", col = test$CatCol,
main = "weight of all samples", border = "NA", origin = 100,

panel = function(x, y, subscripts, ...) {
panel.grid(h = 0, v = -1, col = "gray")
panel.barchart(x, y, ...)
panel.text((x * 1.01), y,
label = paste(test$weightcount[subscripts]),
cex = 0.7)
})

## create a simple plot of just the ratings
rating.plot <- barchart(Product ~ Rating, data = test,
layout = c(1, 1), stack = FALSE, rectangles = TRUE, horizontal = TRUE,
ylab = "Product", xlab = "weight", col = test$CatCol,
main = "Rating of all samples", border = "NA", origin = 0,
panel = function(x, y, subscripts, ...) {
panel.grid(h = 0, v = -1, col = "gray")
panel.barchart(x, y, ...)
panel.text((x * 1.01), y,
label = paste(test$ratingcount[subscripts]),
cex = 0.7)
})


## Print the plots to the default device
print(both.plots)
print(weight.plot)
print(rating.plot)

Hi:

Since you asked this on the ggplot2 list, it's only fair to give one
ggplot2 solution. Josh did a great job showing you the lattice
solution, which probably took a while, so I thought I'd pick up where
he left off :) This isn't as trivial as it seems at first; the trick
is to use geom_segment(), but that geom assumes a numeric x and
numeric y, so we have to add a couple more variables to the mix. Just
as an alternative, I show one way to get (almost) the same data frame
as Josh's ltest using the reshape package's melt() function, although
it's not quite as elegant as Josh's reshape() function solution, which
is worth knowing BTW. [I've seen a way to do it with nested melt's
before in this group, but I haven't hunted it down yet since I was
occupied with the graph.]

[I didn't add the CatCol column because it isn't necessary in ggplot2,
but it is useful in the lattice call.]

# Start with your data frame test:
library(ggplot2) # also loads reshape and plyr

# Josh's definition for ordering levels of product by weight
test$Product <- with(test, factor(Product,
levels = Product[order(Category, weight)]))

# A useful function from the plyr package to rename variables
# Would also be useful to rename 'Catergory' :)
# You need to assign the result of rename(), otherwise it will just
print and not keep the result
test <- rename(test, c('weight' = 'Weight'))

# Melt the data to combine Rating and Weight variables (to use as a
facet variable)
testa <- melt(test, id = c('Catergory', 'Product'),
measure = c('Rating', 'Weight'))

# Count stacks the ratingcount and weightcount variables, but
# you need to make sure you have the right order...not 'safe'
testa$Count <- with(test, c(ratingcount, weightcount))

# Two new variables: a numeric version of Product and a numeric
variable to define
# the 'origin' of the bars for each variable
testa$product <- as.numeric(testa$Product)
testa$origin <- 100 * as.numeric(testa$variable == 'Weight')

## Base version of plot:
g <- ggplot(testa, aes(x = product, y = value))

g + geom_segment(aes(xend = product,
yend = origin,
colour = Catergory), size = 5) +
scale_x_continuous('Product', breaks = unique(testa$product),
labels = levels(testa$Product)) +
theme_bw() +
ylab("Product\n") + xlab('Value') +
geom_text(aes(y = value + sign(value - origin), label = Count), size = 3) +
coord_flip() + facet_wrap(~ variable, nrow = 1, scales= 'free') +
scale_colour_manual(values = c('A' = 'purple', 'B' = 'blue', C= 'green')) +
opts(legend.position = 'none', title = "Weight and rating of all samples")


It looks pretty much the same as the lattice graph, but keeps the
guidelines. I also did a little work to space the locations of the
count labels away from the bars.

Dennis

Dennis
